title: U.S. stock futures slide on calls to slow AI development, M.East escalation
full_text:
Oil prices jump over 3% on more M.East action, Hormuz meeting delay
Investing.com-- U.S. stock index futures fell sharply on Sunday evening with technology on the backfoot amid growing calls to slow the pace of artificial intelligence development.
Markets were also spooked by a surge in oil prices amid worsening tensions in the Middle East, especially after attacks by Yemen’s Houthi group disrupted another major shipping lane in the region.
S&P 500 Futures fell 0.55% to 7,685.75 points by 19:06 ET (23:06 GMT). Nasdaq 100 Futures slid 1.2% to 29,321.0 points, while Dow Jones Futures fell 0.28% to 52,856.0 points.
Futures fell following a positive Friday session on Wall Street as markets were cheered by some declines in oil prices, which faced profit-taking after a strong run-up last week. But oil surged back to near recent peaks on Sunday evening.
Focus this week is squarely on a Federal Reserve meeting where an increasing number of participants believe the central bank will raise interest rates by at least 25 basis points. Rate hike anxiety was also a major weight on Wall Street, especially following upbeat producer and consumer inflation prints released last week.
Get more insights on Wall St and the AI trade with InvestingPro-- up to 50% off
Altman, Musk join calls to slow AI development pace
Tech was set to be the worst performer on Monday after major figures in the AI industry– mainly OpenAI CEO and Sam Altman and Tesla head Elon Musk voiced support for a call to slow down the pace of development.
The two voiced support for Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s call for such a move, after he proposed a sweeping plan to set up more safety practices around AI development.
Separately, AI aggregator Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue, and Google Deepmind Chair Demis Hassabis also supported Amodei’s plan.
Amodei’s call comes following several high-profile hacks that were allegedly carried out by AI agents.
But any slowing in AI development bodes poorly for the stock market, given the trillions of dollars in valuation gains driven by AI over the past four years. Several Wall Street giants– specifically chipmakers and data center developers– are heavily exposed to AI.
M.East escalation boosts oil, spooks Wall St
Oil prices rose sharply on Sunday evening/early Monday after Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked more Saudi Arabian targets over the weekend.
The group also secured a major position along the Bab el-Mandeb strait– a development that heralds renewed disruptions in shipping in the Red Sea.
The Houthi’s actions could cut off another 4%-5% of global oil supplies, given that the Bab el-Mandeb was also an alternative supply channel to the Strait of Hormuz.
The latter also remained shut amid more U.S.-Iran military action over the weekend. Separately, Oman said a meeting between Iran and Gulf powers, to discuss reopening Hormuz, was indefinitely delayed after initially being scheduled for Monday.
Oil prices surged after logging strong gains last week, keeping markets on edge over energy-fueled inflation and its effects on interest rates.

title: Asia tech, chip stocks tumble as AI trade doubts deepen before Fed, BOJ decisions
full_text:
Oil prices jump over 3% on more M.East action, Hormuz meeting delay
Investing.com -- Asian technology stocks fell sharply on Monday, with South Korea’s KOSPI leading the decline, as investors pared exposure to AI-linked chipmakers amid rising bond yields and renewed concerns over the sustainability of the AI rally ahead of key central bank meetings this week.
The tech-heavy KOSPI fell 3.1%, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 slipped 1.1%.
U.S. tech sentiment also remained weak, with Nasdaq 100 futures falling 1.2%, outpacing the 0.4% decline in S&P 500 futures, pointing to continued pressure on growth stocks before Wall Street opens.
The selloff comes after U.S. Treasury yields climbed toward 5% and markets priced in an 86% chance of a 25-basis-point Federal Reserve rate hike this week following hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data.
Higher yields tend to weigh disproportionately on richly valued technology companies whose earnings are expected further into the future.
Semiconductor stocks remained at the center of the pullback, with investors growing more cautious toward the AI trade after a period of outsized gains.
The sector also faced fresh debate over AI spending after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing development of increasingly powerful AI models on safety grounds, comments that added to existing concerns over lofty valuations across AI infrastructure stocks.
South Korea’s technology sector remains particularly sensitive to shifts in AI sentiment because memory-chip giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are major suppliers of high-bandwidth memory used in AI processors.
Chip stocks led losses, with SK Hynix falling 4.3% and Samsung Electronics down 2.5%, weighing on the KOSPI, which was down 3.1%. LG Innotek fell 3.1%, adding to pressure across technology hardware stocks.
Japanese chip-related shares also came under pressure, with the broader semiconductor complex weakening as investors rotated out of high-growth technology names amid rising borrowing costs and geopolitical uncertainty.
Japanese technology stocks were also lower, led by Kioxia, which slumped 7.1%, while Murata Manufacturing fell 3.6% and TDK slipped 0.1%. Sony bucked the trend, rising 3.1%, limiting losses among some large-cap electronics names.
The technology selloff unfolded against a broader risk-off backdrop after oil prices surged above $100 per barrel following renewed attacks involving Saudi energy infrastructure and Gulf shipping, raising fears that inflation could remain elevated and keep central banks on a tighter policy path.
Markets are now awaiting policy decisions from both the Federal Reserve on Wednesday and the Bank of Japan on Friday, with traders also pricing a high probability of a BOJ rate hike that has supported the yen and added further pressure to Japanese equities.

title: Gold slips as hotter US inflation lifts Fed hike bets, oil stokes price pressures
full_text:
Oil prices jump over 3% on more M.East action, Hormuz meeting delay
Investing.com -- Gold prices edged lower on Monday after hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data increased expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates later this week, while surging oil prices added to inflation risks.
Gold was trading near $4,340 an ounce after falling for a third straight week, with bullion down 1.8% last week despite ending Friday’s session higher.
At 21:29 ET (01:29 GMT), XAU/USD fell 0.3% to $4,335.98 an ounce, while Gold Futures declined 0.7% to $4,376.92. XAG/USD fell 0.7% to $64.09 an ounce, while XPT/USD declined 0.3% to $1,792.63. The US Dollar Index rose marginally by 0.1% to 99.19.
Hotter inflation boosts Fed hike expectations
The latest pressure followed August inflation data showing the core consumer price index rose 0.3% month on month, excluding food and energy costs. The increase added to expectations that the Fed could deliver its first rate hike in three years at this week’s meeting.
Markets are now pricing roughly an 88% probability of a September rate increase. Higher borrowing costs typically weigh on gold because the metal generates no interest, making yield producing assets more attractive.
A rate increase could also create political tension for the Fed. President Donald Trump reiterated his calls for lower interest rates on Sunday, continuing his recent criticism of the central bank’s policy stance.
At the same time, the inflation outlook is being complicated by the Middle East conflict. Brent crude climbed toward $107 a barrel after rising almost 9% last week, as the conflict continued to disrupt energy markets.
A meeting planned for Monday between Iran and several Gulf nations to establish a temporary shipping lane through the Strait of Hormuz was postponed, leaving efforts to increase shipments through the critical waterway uncertain.
ANZ sees longer-term support despite rate risks
Gold has traded in a relatively narrow range around $4,400 since rebounding from a floor near $4,000 in July, as investors repeatedly reassessed the outlook for Fed policy.
ANZ said it remains constructive on gold despite expectations for further monetary tightening.
The bank expects escalating Middle East tensions and higher energy prices to drive inflation higher and forecasts three 25 basis point Fed rate hikes by March 2027.
However, ANZ said those inflation pressures are being driven by geopolitical disruptions, which it believes should preserve gold’s safe haven appeal. The bank therefore maintained its 12-month gold price target at $5,400 an ounce.
Investment demand is providing another source of support.
ANZ said gold ETF holdings and speculative positions have recovered in recent months, while strong institutional demand in China and increasing investor participation in India are also supporting the market.

title: Goldman Sachs flips forecast, now sees September Fed rate hike
full_text:
Sept 13 (Reuters) - Goldman Sachs expects the U.S. Federal Reserve to raise interest rates by 25 basis points at its September meeting, joining a growing number of Wall Street firms that see further policy tightening as inflation concerns persist.
In a note on Friday, the brokerage reversed its previous call for the Fed to keep rates unchanged, citing markets pricing that points to a high probability of a rate hike and policymakers’ likely reluctance to surprise investors with a pause.
Goldman Sachs said the shift was driven primarily by market pricing rather than a significant change in its economic outlook, adding that the recent surge in oil prices could make some policymakers more inclined to support additional tightening.
The revised forecast comes as stronger-than-expected U.S. producer price data and a surge in oil prices above $100 a barrel have rekindled inflation concerns, prompting investors and some brokerages to raise bets that the Fed may need to tighten policy further.
Markets are pricing in an 87% chance of a quarter-point Fed rate hike this month, up from roughly 70% prior to the latest data releases, and also expect another increase in December, according to CME’s FedWatch Tool.

title: Anthropic CEO calls for slower AI development after security incidents
full_text:
Oil prices jump over 3% on more M.East action, Hormuz meeting delay
Investing.com -- Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on Saturday for the pace of artificial intelligence development to be slowed, citing an incident in which AI agents from OpenAI and Hugging Face conducted unauthorized cybersecurity attacks on unrelated targets and attempted to hack the system evaluating their performance.
Amodei said the incident, which he referred to as the "OpenAI-Hugging Face incident" or "OAI-HF," involved a swarm of agents that acted "as a fanatically devoted collective," attacking targets they were not asked to attack.
He said "similar, though less severe, incidents have happened across the industry, including at Anthropic."
Amodei said his second concern driving the call to slow down was recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems build the next generation of AI, a dynamic he said is "starting to happen across the industry, including at Anthropic."
He said no one was hurt and the economic damage from the OAI-HF incident was minimal, but a swarm with greater capabilities and similar misalignment "could have caused catastrophic damage."
He said he worries that within six to 12 months, such a swarm could be capable of "taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet," potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage.
Amodei proposed a three-step plan to "pace the frontier." As the first step, Anthropic is unilaterally committing to give an embedded team of third-party evaluators, such as METR, "ongoing, employee-like access" to verify the company’s safety practices and assess the alignment of its models and training pipelines.
The evaluators will receive desks, access badges, company laptops and workspace access "mostly comparable" to internal risk assessment teams, according to the essay.
Anthropic said the evaluators will have the right to publish findings "without editorial control by Anthropic," with narrow exceptions for redacting security-sensitive, legally privileged or confidential information.
The second step calls for frontier AI companies within democratic countries to coordinate on common safety standards and limits on the rate of AI progress.
The third calls for the United States and other democratic governments to attempt coordination with authoritarian governments.
Amodei said pacing does not mean "halting model training or technical progress," but ensuring companies take adequate time to align and safeguard their models.
He said recent alignment incidents were caused "in part by imperfect filtering of broken reinforcement learning environments," an effort he said Anthropic and its vendors "executed reasonably diligently, but not well enough."
Amodei said the United States should not sell powerful AI chips or semiconductor manufacturing equipment to China, should crack down on chip smuggling and unauthorized distillation, and should strengthen security at AI companies to prevent model weight theft, in order to preserve the AI lead of democracies over autocracies.

title: Z.AI shares fall to 5-1/2-month low after $5 billion share, bond sale
full_text:
Oil prices jump over 3% on more M.East action, Hormuz meeting delay
Investing.com -- Z.AI shares fell nearly 7% on Monday to a 5-1/2-month low after the Chinese artificial-intelligence developer launched a roughly $5 billion fundraising that included a discounted share placement and convertible bond sale.
The stock fell to HK$739, its lowest level since March 31, underperforming the broader Hang Seng Index, which was largely unchanged.
The company completed a fundraising comprising about $2 billion from new shares and $3 billion from convertible bonds. The stock has now fallen sharply from its 2026 peak, reflecting a broader pullback in investor enthusiasm for high-valued Chinese AI companies.
The company sold 21.97 million new Hong Kong shares at HK$714 each, a roughly 10% discount to its previous close of HK$793.
It also issued 20.14 billion yuan ($3 billion) of zero-coupon convertible bonds due in September 2027, with an initial conversion price of HK$892.50, a 25% premium to the placement price.
The discounted equity sale is likely to weigh on the shares because it immediately increases the number of shares outstanding, while the convertible bonds could create additional dilution in the future if converted into equity.
However, the higher conversion price means that any eventual conversion would occur only if the stock recovers materially from current levels.
AI spending needs drive fundraising
The fundraising highlights the enormous capital requirements facing AI developers as they expand computing capacity and develop increasingly sophisticated models.
About 60% of Z.AI's net proceeds will go toward research and development of next-generation models and its fully self-training system, while another 15% is earmarked for expansion.
The remainder will be used to optimize its capital structure, replenish working capital and for other corporate purposes.
The new capital gives Z.AI substantially more financial firepower to invest in computing infrastructure and AI development as it competes with Chinese rivals including DeepSeek, Moonshot AI and MiniMax, as well as U.S. companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google.
Z.AI raised about $4 billion in a follow-on share sale in July, meaning the latest financing comes only around two months later.

title: Agentic commerce: Is Payments the winner this time?
full_text:
Oil prices jump over 3% on more M.East action, Hormuz meeting delay
Investing.com -- Agentic commerce accounts for less than 1% of overall e-commerce activity, even as new AI shopping tools from Meta and Anthropic launched this week.
Meta launched Muse, a personal AI agent capable of autonomously executing multistep tasks including email, travel booking, shopping and project management.
Anthropic launched Commerce Agents, an open-source framework designed to help companies build consumer shopping agents and merchant-side operational agents rather than a standalone shopping assistant.
A messaging-first personal AI agent called Instinct, which allows users to text or call to delegate online errands, has also gone viral, at least in Silicon Valley.
The launches follow OpenAI’s abandonment of its Instant Checkout feature, while Google has focused more on infrastructure and standards than on controlling agentic payments, the note said.
Agentic commerce is often discussed as a potential risk for Visa and Mastercard, but "it’s very much the opposite," analysts at Bernstein said, citing more digitization, transactions and value-added services.
Cards will remain the payment method of choice in the agentic world given their dispute management, standards and more than 7 billion credentials and 100 million-plus merchants, the firm said. "Any entity that tries to disintermediate cards for agentic payments is likely doomed."
None of the recent agent launches currently seek to control merchant payments, instead offering frictionless ways for consumers to execute purchases, such as through single-use virtual cards for Muse, the note said.
Visa and Mastercard have developed their own agentic tokens and standards, including Trusted Agent Protocol, Verifiable Intent, Agent Pay and Intelligent Commerce. Bernstein said 100% of agentic transactions will be tokenized.
Agent-to-agent micro-payments remain in the "proof-of-concept stage," Bernstein said, citing the x402 protocol launched by Coinbase and Cloudflare.
The protocol has generated roughly $0.5 million to $1 million in monthly volume a year after launch, with average transaction sizes of about $0.20.
Agentic commerce also means more complexity for merchants, creating a differentiation opportunity for processors such as Adyen, Bernstein said. Adyen launched Adyen Agentic this summer to let enterprises sell through AI platforms without rebuilding commerce systems for each new channel.
GenAI referral traffic as a share of total referrals has risen sharply over the past two years, reaching 39% for Wayfair, 28% for Walmart, 25% for Target, 23% for Etsy and 22% for eBay as of August 2026.
However, the traffic represents only 1-2% of total traffic for these retailers. A Visa survey cited in the note found only 23% of consumers trust AI agents to conduct payment transactions on their behalf.
Bernstein rates Visa, Mastercard and Adyen "outperform."

title: AI leaders raise safety concerns; Hormuz talks delayed - what’s moving markets
full_text:
European stocks slip on AI safety pause, Fed rate bets weigh on sentiment
Investing.com - Futures connected to the main U.S. stock indices edge lower after comments from a high-profile artificial intelligence industry executive raises new concerns about the safety of AI. Stocks in Asia and Europe dip below the flatline, as the statements push traders to recalibrate their expectations for runaway spending on AI infrastructure. Elsewhere, oil prices surge following the delay of a critical meeting between Gulf countries and Iran.
1. Futures retreat
U.S. stock futures pointed lower on Monday, suggesting a downbeat start to the trading week as investors assessed C-suite-level calls for a slowdown the development of artificial intelligence models and prepared for a much-anticipated Federal Reserve interest rate decision.
By 03:04 ET (07:04 GMT), the Dow futures contract had fallen by 63 points, or 0.1%, S&P 500 futures had dropped by 46 points, or 0.6%, and Nasdaq 100 futures had slumped by 431 points, or 1.5%.
Equities on Wall Street ended the prior week in the green, buoyed in part by hopes that a potential meeting between leaders from Gulf countries and Iran will lead to a deal to reopen tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. Oil prices retreated, but remained above the $100 a barrel level. However, the outlook for those talks has since darkened (more below).
Elsewhere, data showing firmer-than-anticipated underlying U.S. consumer price growth in August helped bolster the case for a Fed rate hike this week, although analysts argued that this could be a relief for traders fretting over the central bank’s credibility and independence.
2. Anthropic’s Amodei calls for AI slowdown
But the topic dominating the discussion on Monday was AI, specifically much-debated comments from Dario Amodei, the CEO of high-profile frontier lab Anthropic.
In an essay published on Saturday, Amodei called on AI firms to decelerate the rate of advancement in the cutting-edge models they are racing to construct and deploy, underlining increasing concerns over the possibility that these systems will be misused.
"Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain," Amodei wrote. The statements came after Anthropic revealed last week that several actors had used its Claude AI models in everything from weapons development to fraud.
Markets took particular note of backing for Amodei’s sentiments from other AI industry tycoons, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and xAI boss Elon Musk, noting that perhaps this could indicate a slowdown in a cycle of massive tech-sector investment in AI infrastructure. Still, as analysts at Deutsche Bank said, Amodei’s essay could just alter the "composition of AI capex rather than its scale," with companies choosing to redirect a greater amount of spending to safety, monitoring and governance.
Crucially, Altman said that OpenAI would not go ahead with a possible blockbuster public offering this year due to safety fears.
AI-linked stocks sank in early Asian trading, with OpenAI-investor SoftBank dropping sharply in Japan and contract chipmaking titan Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company dipping. Chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics in South Korea fell as well, while stocks in Europe were also under pressure.
3. Trump says "negative forces" exaggerating AI concerns
President Donald Trump on Sunday said he wants to ensure that the U.S. would maintain its lead over China in the artificial intelligence industry.
“We’re leading China in AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world and, frankly, I want to keep it that way -- because whoever wins AI wins,” Trump told reporters in Ireland when asked whether the industry should slow down or be subject to more regulation.
“We can put guardrails, we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up, and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen,” the U.S. leader added.
4. Gulf leaders postpone Iran meeting over Hormuz proposal
Beyond AI, diplomatic efforts to quell a longstanding conflict in the Middle East and restart activity in a vital oil shipping lane appeared to stumble.
The meeting between Gulf powers and Iran which had eased some worries among investors last week has been postponed. The foreign minister of Oman, who has been seeking a deal over the Strait of Hormuz with Tehran, said the regional gathering was delayed "in the interests of consensus."
Iran’s foreign ministry added that the country would coordinate with Oman to set up another suitable date for the meeting, according to Fars news agency. Previously, Iranian officials had said they would present an agreement with Oman to Gulf Arab states on reopening Hormuz, a narrow waterway bordered by Iran and Oman through which roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas flowed before fresh fighting in the Middle East began in late February.
At the same time, strikes on Saudi Arabia by Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen caused the closure of a critical east-west oil pipeline, while attacks on vessels in the Gulf threatened to compound supply disruptions.
5. Oil prices jump
As a result, oil prices rose sharply early on Monday. Brent crude futures, the global oil benchmark, briefly surpassed $108 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures also jumped.

Amodei’s essay proposed a plan to "pace the frontier," following public resignations of safety and alignment staff at some major AI labs who were reportedly unsatisfied with existing safeguards. His comments were echoed by Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Satya Nadella and other industry figures.
Bernstein analysts led by Stacy Rasgon said they expect the news to "have potential to further depress sentiment" on the semiconductor group, which had been recovering after falling roughly 19% from its June peak.

Memory makers appear particularly exposed to any AI slowdown. Unlike fabless IP provider Arm, which carries software-like margins, or ASML, which has a multi-year equipment backlog, margin expansion at SK Hynix, Samsung Electronics and Micron has been driven largely by tight high-bandwidth memory (HBM) supply and favorable pricing, leaving their earnings more sensitive to any pullback in AI capital spending.
Still, expanding inference demand and multi-quarter supply agreements could cushion HBM sales initially even if AI development slows, delaying any hit to margins unless weaker demand eventually leads to rising inventories and softer pricing.
Bernstein analysts said they do not believe a "pacing slowdown" necessarily implies a spending slowdown. The team noted Amodei is not calling for a halt to training, but rather a shift from "extremely fast" to "only somewhat fast", a pace the analysts said would still represent significant growth. They also pointed to rising AI demand from inference and agentic use cases, noting there is "already not nearly enough compute to satisfy demand for even the current models."
Bernstein also questioned how much of the proposal is driven by competition with China, noting Amodei’s plan includes continued restrictions on selling advanced AI chips and equipment to Chinese firms, along with cracking down on unauthorized AI model distillation.
Anthropic’s own spending has shown no signs of slowing. The Financial Times reported that Anthropic expects a second consecutive quarter of adjusted operating profit, with inference gross margins exceeding 80% before distribution costs.
Looking ahead, Bernstein said it remains positive on AI buildout prospects, naming Nvidia, Broadcom and semiconductor capital equipment makers as its preferred plays in the sector.

title: Anthropic wants AI to slow down. Its $517 billion spending plan says otherwise
full_text:
European stocks slip on AI safety pause, Fed rate bets weigh on sentiment
Investing.com - Anthropic agreed to $517 billion in compute commitments covering 14.8 gigawatts of capacity in the 11 months through August 2026, according to The Information, even as its CEO publicly called on the industry to pump the brakes on AI development.
Nvidia, which is reportedly in talks to invest up to $10 billion as an anchor investor in Anthropic's expected Nasdaq IPO, is the most direct equity expression of that dynamic: every gigawatt Anthropic contracts translates into accelerated GPU and networking demand that flows straight to Nvidia's data-center revenue line.
The scale of Anthropic's compute commitments dwarfs a prior investor disclosure of roughly $180 billion through 2029, with four additional deals struck since July alone, The Information reported. That capital outlay is increasingly backed by real economics.
Anthropic told investors it expects a second consecutive quarter of adjusted operating profit, and inference gross margins exceeded 80% before distribution costs, the Financial Times said, citing investor briefings that Anthropic has not confirmed on the record. The company's revenue run rate climbed from roughly $9 billion to $65 billion in seven months, according to the same FT account.
The contrast with the rhetoric landing on the same week sharpened the tension considerably. On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay calling on AI labs to "slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models," proposing embedded third-party evaluators, industry-wide safety standards, and global coordination.
"Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain," Amodei wrote. OpenAI's Sam Altman and Elon Musk both publicly endorsed the framework.
"I don't know that investors are necessarily going to see it as a negative. Unless the companies are genuine and say, 'OK, we're not going to IPO, we're not going to use any more compute, we're not going to train any more models.' That's not what they're saying," Gil Luria, equity analyst at D.A. Davidson, told CNBC.
The market read the slowdown rhetoric with skepticism. AI-linked Asian stocks slumped following the Amodei' statements, and Wall Street's AI trade came under scrutiny. But the broader infrastructure thesis appeared intact.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, speaking at Goldman Sachs's tech conference last week, forecast global AI infrastructure spending of $3 trillion to $4 trillion by 2030 and said Nvidia's roughly 70% fiscal 2027 revenue growth reflects a supply ceiling rather than a demand limit. His prior projections proved conservative: a February 2024 forecast that the world's installed data-center base would double within four to five years was reached by end of 2025.
On the IPO front, OpenAI will not go public in 2026. "Right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public. I would say not 2026, yeah. We got a lot of stuff to do," Altman said.
Anthropic is moving in the opposite direction, having confidentially filed its IPO prospectus with the SEC in June 2026. Sources cited by Reuters put its target valuation at around $2 trillion, a significant step up from its most recent private funding round valuation of $965 billion, with listing timing expected before the U.S. midterm elections in November 2026.
The offering would be among the largest in history and deliver the first GAAP-audited look at Anthropic's revenue and compute-cost structure. Nvidia's reported anchor bid of up to $10 billion would cement the chipmaker's strategic relationship with one of its largest customers while giving it direct upside in the lab's equity.
China's state-backed Global Times dismissed Amodei's slowdown call as a "Cold War playbook" targeting Beijing, underscoring that any coordinated Western pacing effort carries geopolitical weight well beyond the balance sheets of the labs involved.
"While the proposal uses fears of RSI and safety/alignment as its hammer, we wonder if China concerns are a large part of the driving force here," Bernstein analysts led by Stacy Rasgon wrote in a note.
"We suspect it is far too late to put the AI genie back in the bottle anyway, so we might as well find safer ways to let it out."

title: Chevron eyes Argentina, Mediterranean for global LNG growth, deal with India
full_text:
European stocks slip on AI safety pause, Fed rate bets weigh on sentiment
By Emily Chow and Florence Tan
BANGKOK, Sept 14 (Reuters) - Chevron is looking to expand its global gas portfolio from Argentina to the Mediterranean to meet growing demand from buyers concerned about energy security due to the crisis in the Middle East, President of Global Gas Freeman Shaheen said.
Global gas markets have experienced two major disruptions in the past four years as the Ukraine war in 2022 and the Iran conflict this year cut off supplies from top producers Russia and Qatar and drove liquefied natural gas prices higher.
"What we’re seeing from this crisis is that it just reinforces the need for diversity — diversity of supply and diversity of different contracting structures," Shaheen said, adding, "and not leaving yourselves susceptible to a spot market that’s not really as liquid as crude and products."
Chevron will have about 20 million metric tons per annum of LNG supply capacity comprising 16 million tons of net gas production from its projects and 4 million tons contracted from the U.S. Gulf Coast that commenced in February this year and will ramp up over the next few years in line with agreements.
"We’re looking to continue to expand that portfolio," Shaheen said in an interview on the sidelines of the Gastech conference in Bangkok.
"There’s great prospects out of Argentina with the development of crude and gas in that marketplace. The East Mediterranean is a very exciting area for us as well."
He also sees further opportunities in Australia and Africa, provided the projects offer the right capital, fiscal and regulatory terms, adding that the U.S.-Iran war has reinforced the need for a diversified gas portfolio.
Shaheen did not elaborate on where in Africa, Australia or the eastern Mediterranean the company might expand. In June, Chevron won approval to become operator and lead gas exploration in an offshore block off Greece, expanding its presence there.
However, these opportunities have to be weighed against Venezuela, where Chevron and its partners would invest more than $7 billion to more than double oil output by 2031.
"I’ve been hearing that Venezuela has a lot of capital that’s going to have to go that way coming up," Shaheen told Reuters.
"Everything is going to get analysed in our project queue and it gets ranked."
Chevron already has significant operations in Australia, running the country’s largest LNG project, Gorgon, and the Wheatstone project. A large portion of its Australian supply goes to Japan.
"Japan continues to be our home base, and we have nice structural opportunities into Singapore," Shaheen said, adding that China and Korea remain attractive markets.
In Singapore, Chevron inked a deal in 2024 to supply Sembcorp Industries up to 0.6 million tons per annum of LNG from 2028.
LNG buyers are also changing the way they secure supply, he said, with state-backed importers increasingly willing to sign contracts with portfolio suppliers rather than relying on government-to-government arrangements.
"I’d love to have a deal in India. It’s just they’re very, very headline-price driven," Shaheen said. "I think India is still evolving. There’s going to be great opportunities over time."

title: Companies left China to dodge tariffs. Now some are heading back
full_text:
European stocks slip on AI safety pause, Fed rate bets weigh on sentiment
By Ellen Zhang and Marius Zaharia
BEIJING/HONG KONG, Sept 14 (Reuters) - A year after shifting production and sourcing out of China to avoid higher U.S. tariffs, some companies are learning that replicating the country’s factory ecosystem is not so easy and are bringing manufacturing back.
Last year, as President Donald Trump’s tariffs set off a global rush to diversify supply chains, Heather Kuang’s China-based metal casting company lost business when a major U.S. customer shifted some orders to India.
The customer has since returned with new orders after running into problems there, said Kuang, vice president of family-owned Dawang Metals, based in the northeastern Chinese city of Dandong. She declined to identify the agricultural machinery company.
Dawang also explored moving some production offshore before abandoning the plan.
"China’s supply-chain advantage is still too great, and it is difficult to replicate domestic production elsewhere," Kuang said.
Companies continue to invest in Southeast Asia’s manufacturing hubs, but the "China plus one" push, under which firms hedged China exposure with operations in other lower-tariff countries, has proved harder to execute.
While there is not yet hard data showing how much sourcing is returning to China, some buyers who shifted production elsewhere said they are keeping or restoring Chinese suppliers because factories abroad struggle to match its skilled labour, supplier networks and reliable power.
Even so, rival manufacturing hubs India, Indonesia and Vietnam have attracted investments from electronics, automotive and other manufacturers despite persistent concerns.
The shifts are unfolding ahead of an expected meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping this month, which businesses will watch for clarity on a proposed mechanism to lower barriers on some non-sensitive goods.
U.S. retailer Target has moved some orders back to Chinese suppliers, two people familiar with the matter said, citing supply-chain disruptions and production constraints. The sources did not disclose the value or duration of the orders.
Shein, the Chinese fast-fashion retailer, is also scaling back some operations in Vietnam, according to people familiar with its operations there.
Target and Shein did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Jin Chaofeng, an exporter of outdoor furniture in Hangzhou, eastern China, said he shut a workshop in Ho Chi Minh City that he opened in 2024 and moved production back to China this year.
He said he had trouble finding the equipment he needed in Vietnam, and needed to bring in basic items from China such as screws and moulds for cup holders.
The arithmetic that once justified moving abroad has changed, he said. "Once I factored everything in, the overall cost was not much different, so there was no point."
One reason for the shift from China was to exploit differences in U.S. tariff rates.
China faced an effective U.S. tariff rate of about 20%, compared with 6.1% for Vietnam, 13.4% for Indonesia and 4.5% for Thailand, according to Economist Intelligence Unit estimates in July. But that advantage has narrowed as Washington extended tariffs to a wider range of countries, prompting some Chinese manufacturers to rethink overseas investment, the EIU said.
BEYOND TARIFFS
Access to power has become as decisive as price, especially after the Middle East crisis tested the energy reliability of manufacturing bases, some companies said.
Stanislaw Krykun, CEO of Poland-based packaging firm DST Pack, worked with his six-year Chinese manufacturing partner to get through the painful period when plastic input costs spiked 15% in April because of soaring oil prices.
"In case of any crisis, the Chinese production plants will be the most stable plants you can use," Krykun said.
DST Pack sources 80% of its production from a factory in Shenzhen, with 10% each from long-established backup plants in the U.S. and Europe, he said.
Those alternatives cost two to three times more per unit.
Krykun had dismissed relocating to Southeast Asia after seeing a business partner struggle in Vietnam. "He faced a lot of issues starting with production and finishing with the export," he said. "The system there doesn’t really work as smoothly as it works in China."
Guan Baokui, a Qingdao-based lawyer who advises manufacturers, said Vietnam and Indonesia suffer from an "unstable and not continuous" electricity supply, a problem that intensified as global oil prices surged.
Not all exporters are seeing U.S. demand return. Summer Hu, a Ningbo-based sales agent for gift and outdoor sports products, said her company had not seen U.S. orders increase.
"We are not that optimistic," Hu said. "The competition is too intense."
Vietnam remains one of the biggest beneficiaries of supply-chain diversification, attracting billions of dollars of foreign investment.
Yu Yangxian, who sells electric lockers and vending machines, said her company is keeping roughly one-eighth of its total capacity in Vietnam as a hedge.
She said the company could expand there again "if Trump goes crazy" and tariffs spike.
Exporters said they do not expect the Trump-Xi summit to resolve their problems.
"We gave up expecting much from Trump long ago. We can’t depend on him for our livelihood or pin all our hopes on him. We have to find export markets to sustain ourselves," Kuang said.

title: Apple: JPM says delivery lead times for iPhone 18 line down from last year
full_text:
European stocks slip on AI safety pause, Fed rate bets weigh on sentiment
Investing.com -- Early delivery lead times for Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are tracking lower than last year’s iPhone 17 launch, JPMorgan says, suggesting some consumers may be holding off in anticipation of the company’s new foldable device. Apple announced the iPhone 18 series on September 9, with the Pro and Pro Max models opening for pre-order on September 12 and general availability beginning September 18.
JPMorgan analysts led by Samik Chatterjee tracked delivery lead times across the U.S., China, Germany, and the U.K. as a demand indicator during the first week of pre-orders. Globally, delivery-at-home timing for the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max averaged 7 and 19 days, respectively, in week one, compared with 15 and 24 days for the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max a year earlier.
"The shortfall relative to last year is more notable in the Pro SKU rather than the Pro Max SKU," the analysts said.
In the U.S., which accounts for about 34% of iPhone shipments, lead times for the 18 Pro and Pro Max came in at 2 and 22 days, versus 4 and 21 days a year ago. JPMorgan noted that Pro Max lead times are "tracking modestly ahead of the prior year even as the Pro tracks lower."
China showed the largest year-over-year shift. Lead times for the 18 Pro and Pro Max tracked at 13 and 21 days, respectively, compared with 30 days each for both iPhone 17 models last year. China represents roughly 19% of iPhone shipments.
JPMorgan said it expects Apple’s foldable phone, called Duo, to gain strong traction there given that Chinese consumers "are already primed for adoption of the foldable form factor" following several years of foldable offerings from domestic manufacturers.
In Europe, Germany saw lead times of 5 and 16 days for the 18 Pro and Pro Max, down from 14 and 22 days a year ago. The U.K. tracked at 9 and 19 days, compared with 14 and 22 days previously. Germany and the U.K. account for about 3% and 4% of iPhone shipments, respectively.
Despite the shorter lead times, the analysts cautioned against reading too much into the data at this early stage. They underscored that "supply allocations across the Pro Max and Pro SKU can be different from prior years" given the absence of a base model launch and the incremental rollout of the foldable device this fall, adding that tracking the trajectory of lead times over time will be important for gauging underlying demand.
